Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes strike the staff on the floor in these Chan records. Its wording is to strike or plant the staff. Frozen-corpus concordance: 5662 exact hits in 309 storage files representing 304 independent works. Records count it once, twice, or three times. Xuzhou Pudu strikes twice and verbally distinguishes smashing to pieces from the words still remaining. Xuanming Foyin strikes during a public exchange and answers the challenge to his extra action. Ciming Chuyuan uses the staff strike to supply the demanded phrase. Other records place it after a pause, beside a shout, immediately before stepping down, or as the staff's announced explanation of the matter. Xueyan Zuqin strikes and supplies the requested phrase in a formal festival address. These observable placements define the Chan use; the entry assigns no unspoken message to a strike.

To take a seat and remain sitting. Chan records use the ordinary bodily action in institutionally loaded scenes without making the bare verb itself a separate technical noun. An unnamed monk sits every day in the sutra hall instead of reading scripture. Xuanquan Yan warns clear-eyed patch-robed monks not to 'sit in the mud.' Yuantong Xiu lists three monks in snow—one sitting with his head covered, one sucking a writing brush and composing poetry, and one sitting around the brazier talking about food—and Baichi Yuan calls the first a board-carrying Chan fellow. Hansong Zhicao permits his assembly to sleep or walk and asks why they must rigidly insist on sitting. Wuzu Fayan speaks of Shuangquan sitting amid commotion, while Fachang Yiyu describes eighteen senior men sitting silently around a brazier. The word itself names the seated bodily action; place, duration, posture, institutional setting, and each named speaker's praise or criticism come from the surrounding sentence.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 322 matches in 132 files. 'Sit every day' occurs seven times in seven files; 'sit with the head covered' eighteen times in fifteen; 'sit around a brazier' thirty-five times in twenty-six; and 'sit in the mud' four times in four. The direct nominal form occurs once, in a question about one sitting on Kunlun Mountain. No other required definition formula occurs. The entry therefore uses the plain English action and preserves the corpus's explicit descriptive and critical modifiers rather than introducing a category absent from the Chinese.

Senses.Explanation: To be made into one piece is to become continuous rather than divided by time, motion and stillness, arising and perishing, or subject and object. The records apply the phrase across sustained inquiry and all twelve periods of daily activity. Zhongfeng Mingben places it after long continuity; Tianyin Yuanxiu requires it through all twelve periods of the day; Weian Deran pairs it with arising and perishing becoming one and motion and stillness not being two. Ruibai Mingxue says subject and object both disappear. A later record quotes Xiangyan Zhixian saying that it took forty years. Yuanwu Keqin uses the phrase as a name for the one-colour side, while Zhongfeng elsewhere rejects calling a consciously recognized silver mountain and iron wall by this name. The negative witness blocks the idea that one merely imagines a separate object and pounds it together.

Senses.Explanation: To manage to say it is to produce an answer that meets the demand of the present exchange. The phrase appears in explicit stakes—sit if you can say it, lose the belt if you cannot—and later verdicts that someone said only half; the longer string meaning 'what did an outsider obtain?' is not this lexical item.
